item.title: Southern University System Presidential Search Committee announces semifinalists
item.description:
The Southern University System Presidential Search Committee today selected semifinalists to advance in the national search for the next president of the Southern University System.

The Search Committee selected the following individuals to advance to the semifinalist stage:

Brian K. Bridges, Ph.D.
Senior Advisor, Whiteboard Advisors
Former Secretary of Higher Education, State of New Jersey (2020-2025)

John K. Belton, J.D.
District Attorney, Third Judicial District Court — Louisiana

Jaffus Hardrick, Ed.D.
Former President, Florida Memorial University 

Roscoe Jones, J.D.
Former Dean, Drake University Law School 

Larissa Littleton-Steib, Ph.D.
Chancellor, Delgado Community College

Willie E. Smith, Ed.D.
Chancellor, Baton Rouge Community College

“Today represents an important milestone in our search for the next president of the Southern University System,” said Jason Hughes, chair, 2026 Southern University System Presidential Search Committee. “Our committee has approached this responsibility thoughtfully and deliberately, recognizing the significance of selecting the individual who will help lead the nation’s only historically Black university system into its next chapter. We are pleased with the progress of the search and look forward to learning more about each of these candidates as we move into the interview phase.”

The selection of semifinalists follows an extensive national search process that has included stakeholder engagement throughout the Southern University System and outreach to prospective candidates. More than 350 students, faculty, staff, administrators, alumni and community stakeholders participated in engagement sessions earlier this year, providing input on the experience, qualities and leadership characteristics desired in the System’s next president.

The Search Committee extends its appreciation to TM² Executive Search, which has assisted the Southern University System throughout the national search process. The firm has worked with the committee to facilitate stakeholder engagement, develop the presidential prospectus, conduct candidate outreach and research, and guide the committee through the evaluation and selection process.

“The committee is grateful to TM² Executive Search for its guidance and expertise throughout this process,” Hughes said. “Their work, along with the valuable input we received from stakeholders across the Southern University System, has helped us conduct a comprehensive search focused on identifying highly qualified leaders who understand both the opportunities and responsibilities associated with leading this historic System.”

Next Steps

The semifinalists will be invited to participate in in-person interviews with the Presidential Search Committee in the coming weeks. Following those interviews, the committee will determine which candidates will advance to the finalist stage of the search process.

Additional information regarding the interview process and subsequent steps in the presidential search will be announced as details are finalized.

The Southern University System launched the national search following the departure of its previous president. The Presidential Search Committee includes representatives from across the Southern University System and the broader community and is charged with recommending finalists for consideration by the Southern University Board of Supervisors.

About the Southern University System

The Southern University System is the nation’s only historically Black university system and includes Southern University and A&M College, Southern University at New Orleans, Southern University at Shreveport, Southern University Law Center and the Southern University Agricultural Research and Extension Center. Through teaching, research and service, the System is committed to providing educational access and opportunity while developing leaders and strengthening communities throughout Louisiana and beyond.

item.title: Southern University System celebrates scholarship support and student success at 2nd annual Southern Celebrates Scholarship Event
item.description:
The Southern University System hosted its second annual Southern Celebrates Scholarship Event Wednesday at the Southern University Welcome Center, bringing together more than 300 benefactors, corporate partners and student scholars from across the Southern University System to celebrate the impact of scholarships, mentorship and partnerships on student success.

The morning brunch highlighted the contributions of supporters whose generosity provides direct support to students at Southern University campuses in Baton Rouge, New Orleans and Shreveport. The event also gave benefactors and corporate partners an opportunity to engage with student scholars and Southern University administrative and academic leaders.

This year’s event also marked Southern University’s 146th year of service to Louisiana and the nation. Southern University is the nation’s only Historically Black College and University system.

“Today is about the gratitude we have for our students who excel and raise the bar,” said Dr. Orlando McMeans, interim president of the Southern University System and chancellor of the Southern University Ag Center. “It is equally about gratitude for those who contribute to that excellence — those who give, mentor, provide a network, an ear, or a prayer. We thank you.”

The program featured a moderated panel discussion, “The Power of Partnership: Nutrien & Southern University,” facilitated by Alfred E. Harrell III, president and CEO of the Southern University System Foundation. Panelists included Ebonie Raby, senior adviser for community relations and investment at Nutrien; Dr. Robert Easley, director of advancement for the College of Agriculture, Human and Environmental Sciences at Southern University and A&M College; and Bryan Glass, a Southern University student scholar.

The discussion highlighted the Nutrien Scholarship Fund at Southern University and explored how sustained corporate-university partnerships can create educational opportunities for students from communities across Louisiana.

“Southern’s success is a shared success,” said Harrell. “Every gift, every mentorship, every partnership represented in this room is already at work in the life of a Southern University student. This event is our opportunity to say thank you, and to show our partners exactly what their investment makes possible.”

The second annual Southern Celebrates Scholarship Event was made possible through the support of Dow, Mele Printing, Aramark, Renasant Bank, the Southern University System Foundation and the Southern University System.

For more information about the Southern University System Foundation and its work supporting donor relations, major gift fundraising, legacy giving and corporate partnerships across the Southern University System, contact Biyaka Williams at biyaka@sutrueblue.org.

item.title: College of Sciences and Engineering to host inaugural STEM game day experience Saturday
item.description:
Southern University’s College of Sciences and Engineering will host its inaugural STEM Game Day, sponsored by Google, on Saturday, Sept. 19, from noon to 4 p.m. at the Southern University Welcome Center. The event will bring science, technology, engineering and mathematics to life through hands-on learning, innovation, gaming and career exploration. All STEM Game Day activities will take place at the Welcome Center, with the exception of the e-sports experience, which will be located on the east side of A.W. Mumford Stadium.

The event reflects Southern University’s commitment to expanding access to STEM education, developing the next generation of STEM professionals and strengthening connections among education, industry and the community.

“STEM Game Day is about creating an environment where students can see, touch and experience STEM while imagining themselves as the scientists, engineers, technologists and innovators of tomorrow,” said Lealon Martin, Ph.D., dean of the College of Sciences and Engineering. “By bringing these experiences into the energy and excitement of Southern University Game Day, we have an opportunity to reach students and families in a unique way while strengthening the connection between our university and the communities we serve.”

Designed to combine the excitement and tradition of Southern University game day with opportunities to explore the possibilities of STEM, the event welcomes K-12 students, families, educators, college students, alumni and community members. Participants will have opportunities to engage with Southern University faculty and students, community organizations and industry professionals through interactive activities and demonstrations.

In addition to Google’s sponsorship, participating community and industry partners include STEM NOLA/STEM Global Action Network, SU EDGE, INDUSTRY MAKES and NOLAvate Black, along with additional Southern University and community partners. Together, the organizations will provide opportunities for students to learn directly from professionals, educators, entrepreneurs and innovators.

A central goal of STEM Game Day is to help young people recognize that STEM extends beyond classrooms and laboratories and plays a role in fields such as gaming, sports, transportation, health care, manufacturing, energy, computing, artificial intelligence and entrepreneurship. By introducing K-12 students to STEM in a fun and welcoming environment, the College of Sciences and Engineering seeks to encourage students to explore STEM coursework, college majors and career opportunities.

College students will also have opportunities to engage with industry and community partners, learn about career pathways and connect their academic experiences to real-world applications. Alumni and community members are invited to participate and support the next generation of STEM leaders.

item.title: SULC Tax Law Clinic Students Explore Legal Matters at Louisiana Board of Tax Appeals
item.description:
From tax credits to civil procedure, ethics and professionalism, Southern University Law Center (SULC) Tax Law students recently explored the complexities of legal practice during a visit with the Louisiana Board of Tax Appeals.

Each student attended hearings featuring legal issues such as historic and motion picture tax credits. The proceedings provided students with a firsthand look into how tax matters are presented and resolved, while also addressing issues of civil procedure, professionalism, and ethics that arose during the hearings.

Students also observed two other proceedings involving self- represented litigants, including an exception of prescription and a follow up status conference on a motion to compel. The cases presented an opportunity for the students to see legal concepts in motion and gain firsthand insight into how key issues can arise in practice.

“Our Tax Law Clinic along with Clinical Tax Professor Christian Fasullo, observed the Louisiana Board of Tax Appeals on September 3. This exciting opportunity exposed our student attorneys to state tax litigation matters, the legal practice, and the tax judicial system in action," said Virginia Listach, SULC Professor and Director of Clinical Legal Education. "As an additional bonus, our clinical students will provide a valuable resource to the tax court by assisting self-represented litigants (SRLs) with tax forms and aid the tax court in the development of a self-help SRL legal resource page.”

After the hearings concluded, the students participated in meaningful discussions that connected the day’s proceedings to their legal education. The Louisiana Board of Tax Appeals chairman provided an overview of the history of the Board, giving insight into its purpose and responsibilities.

During the visit, they also discussed the self-represented litigants and received an overview of taxation in Louisiana and the application of tax credits. 

Students within SULC’s Tax Law Clinic will continue their hands-on learning with the Louisiana Board of Tax Appeals during hearings in October and November.

Experiential learning opportunities such as this allow SULC students to see how legal concepts discussed in the classroom translate into real-world practice. By observing proceedings and engaging in discussions with legal professionals, students can further develop the knowledge and skills needed to become practice-ready attorneys.

item.title: Updated Louisiana law heightens penalties for marijuana use on college campuses
item.description:
FROM THE OFFICE OF LOUISIANA GOVERNOR JEFF LANDRY

MARIJUANA ON CAMPUS IS A CRIME

LOUISIANA LAW CHANGED ON AUGUST 1, 2026

 

WHERE THE LAW APPLIES

On campus property. Within 2,000 feet of campus property.

The statute defines "school" to include any public or private college or university in Louisiana and any vocational- technical school. It reaches any person, so it applies to employees and visitors as well as students.

La. R.S. 40:981.3(A), (C)(1)

 

WHAT CHANGED ON AUGUST 1, 2026

Act 305 of the 2026 Regular Session set a new penalty for marijuana possession in a school zone: imprisonment, with or without hard labor, for up to one year, plus a fine of up to $1,000. Before August 1, possessing 14 grams or less carried a fine of up to $100.

La. R.S. 40:981.3(E); La. R.S. 40:966(C)(2)(a)(i)

 

THE ZONE REACHES WELL PAST CAMPUS

Two thousand feet is more than a third of a mile measured out from the property line. On most Louisiana campuses that ring takes in apartments, dorms, fraternity and sorority houses, parking and tailgating lots.

La. R.S. 40:981.3(A)(1)

 

SMOKING AND VAPING ARE COVERED

Act 305 added a new paragraph reaching anyone who violates the drug laws "while smoking, vaping, or otherwise abusing" a controlled dangerous substance in these locations. A THC vape pen counts. Students or guests who possess a prescription order to possess marijuana are not exempt from legal recourse if smoking on school property. La. R.S. 40:981.3(A)(4)

 

THIS IS FELONY-LEVEL EXPOSURE

Louisiana defines a felony as any crime for which the offender may be sentenced to imprisonment at hard labor. The new penalty allows a sentence at hard labor. A conviction goes on an adult criminal record.

La. R.S. 14:2(4)

 

"I DIDN'T KNOW I WAS NEAR A SCHOOL" IS NOT A DEFENSE

The statute states that lack of knowledge that the act occurred on or within 2,000 feet of school property is not a defense.

La. R.S. 40:981.3(B)

 

PENALTIES

UP TO ONE YEAR IN PRISON 

With or without hard labor.

UP TO A $1,000 FINE 

In addition to imprisonment.

Lacumba’s Lair will feature Louisiana-inspired cuisine, beverages, a live DJ and musical entertainment, interactive activations, game-viewing screens, photo opportunities, and indoor and outdoor hospitality spaces. Guests may choose between the Lair Experience and a limited-availability Premium Lair Experience, which includes preferred parking, reserved seating, premium hospitality and an exclusive game-day experience.

Advance ticket purchase is required, and guests are asked to wear white, the color of the first home football game of the season. Football game tickets or access to the A.W. Mumford Stadium are not included with the Lacumba’s Lair experience.

Proceeds from Lacumba’s Lair will support the Chancellor’s Access and Opportunity Fund.

item.title: SULC Faculty Share Expertise at 2026 SEALS Annual Conference
item.description:
Southern University Law Center Professors Donna Schwab, Judd Sneirson, and Carlo Pedrioli represented SULC at the 2026 Southeastern Association of Law Schools (SEALS) Annual Conference in Amelia Island, Florida.

Professor Schwab participated in the discussion group “Teaching and Researching in Civil and Comparative Law,” while Professor Sneirson participated in the discussion “Corporate Purpose and Misconduct” and a New Scholars Panel. Professor Pedrioli coordinated and co-chaired the discussion “Voting Rights and Redistricting: The U.S. Supreme Court Decides Louisiana v. Callais.” 

They also explored emerging topics in the legal field, including AI and the NextGen Bar Exam.

We’re proud to see our faculty contributing to important conversations shaping the future of legal education and the legal profession!

item.title: Southern University System strengthens partnership with St. Kitts and Nevis during official visit
item.description:
The Southern University System continued to advance its growing international partnership with the Federation of St. Kitts and Nevis during an official visit to the Caribbean nation, where Interim President Orlando F. McMeans met June 25 with Prime Minister Dr. Terrance Michael Drew to discuss expanding collaboration in higher education, agriculture, research and workforce development.

The meeting provided Interim President McMeans and Prime Minister Drew an opportunity to reaffirm their shared commitment to expanding educational access and developing innovative partnerships that promote economic growth, workforce development and sustainable progress throughout the Caribbean. The discussions also included Her Excellency Dr. Hadiya Claxton, whose leadership has been instrumental in advancing educational and international business relations for the Federation of St. Kitts and Nevis.

“This visit reflects our continued commitment to building meaningful partnerships that create opportunities for our students, strengthen communities and address global challenges,” McMeans said. “Our collaboration with St. Kitts and Nevis demonstrates what is possible when higher education, government and industry work together. We are not only expanding access to higher education across the Southern University System but also advancing sustainable agriculture, food security, research and workforce development throughout the Caribbean.”

The visit further strengthened the strategic relationship between the Southern University System and the Government of St. Kitts and Nevis through collaborative initiatives that expand educational opportunities, advance agricultural innovation and foster long-term economic development.

Central to those efforts is the memorandum of understanding between the Southern University System and the Ministry of Education of the Federation of St. Kitts and Nevis, which continues to expand access to higher education for students from the island nation while strengthening academic, research and cultural collaboration between Southern University and the Federation.

The partnership also extends beyond higher education through the Southern University Agricultural Research and Extension Center. Under a separate memorandum of understanding, the Ag Center provides sustainable and environmental agriculture consulting services to the Ministry of Agriculture under the leadership of the Honorable Samal Duggins. The collaboration equips the Federation's farming community with research-based expertise and innovative practices that strengthen agricultural sustainability, enhance food security and advance agricultural research throughout the region.

Building on the success of its partnership with St. Kitts and Nevis, the Southern University System is exploring opportunities to establish similar collaborations with Jamaica, Saint Lucia, The Bahamas, Bermuda, and Antigua and Barbuda. These efforts reflect the System's commitment to expanding its global reach and serving as a leader in higher education, research, agricultural innovation and international engagement.

The partnership will continue this fall as the Southern University System welcomes its newest Class of 2030 from St. Kitts and Nevis. Among the incoming students is the reigning Miss St. Kitts, whose decision to enroll at Southern reflects the university system's growing international reputation.

As the Southern University System continues to expand its global footprint, its partnership with St. Kitts and Nevis serves as a model for international collaboration by creating educational opportunities, advancing research and agricultural innovation, and strengthening communities throughout the Caribbean and beyond.

item.title: Southern University System names Ronald Solomon as chief information officer
item.description:
The Southern University System has appointed Ronald Solomon as chief information officer (CIO), bringing more than three decades of experience in information technology leadership, enterprise systems management, cybersecurity, and strategic planning to the nation’s only historically Black university system.

Solomon was selected following a national search conducted with the assistance of TM² Executive Search, the firm retained by the System to support executive recruitment efforts. Through a comprehensive search process, TM² identified and evaluated highly qualified candidates, ultimately yielding a strong pool of professionals from which Solomon emerged as the successful candidate.

As CIO, Solomon will lead the System’s technology strategy, infrastructure, cybersecurity initiatives, enterprise applications, and digital transformation efforts in support of more than 14,000 students, faculty, and staff across the System’s five campuses.

“The chief information officer plays a critical role in ensuring that Southern University remains secure and responsive to the evolving needs of higher education,” said Orlando F. McMeans, interim president of the Southern University System. “We are grateful to TM² Executive Search for assisting us in identifying an outstanding candidate in Mr. Solomon. His extensive experience and strategic vision make him exceptionally well-suited to guide our technology initiatives as we continue to strengthen and modernize our institutions.”

Solomon joins Southern after serving as CIO at Baton Rouge Community College, where he led strategic technology planning aligned with institutional and statewide goals. During his tenure, he oversaw Banner ERP operations, data governance, cybersecurity programs, infrastructure modernization, network operations, and technology procurement while advancing collaboration and shared services across higher education institutions.

An accomplished technology executive, Solomon is recognized for leading system-wide IT governance, modernization initiatives, cloud migration projects and cybersecurity improvements. His work has focused on aligning technology investments with institutional priorities while enhancing operational resilience, improving user experiences and strengthening cybersecurity governance.

Solomon earned a Master of Science degree in computer science from Colorado Technical University and a Bachelor of Science degree in computer science from McNeese State University. He is an Oracle Certified Professional and serves in several statewide technology leadership roles, including vice chair of the State CIO Group. He is a member of the Louisiana Community and Technical College System Cybersecurity Committee and the Council of Information Services Directors.

item.title: Southern University Board of Supervisors approves resolution to establish law school in Shreveport
item.description:
The Southern University Board of Supervisors has unanimously approved a resolution to establish a law school in Shreveport, Louisiana, marking a significant step toward expanding access to legal education in North Louisiana.

The action came during the Board’s April meeting held in Shreveport, where members also received a comprehensive report from an external consultant outlining the feasibility of and demand for a law program in the Northwest Louisiana region. The report highlighted strong regional need, workforce demand, and the opportunity to broaden the pipeline of legal professionals serving the area.

“This is a bold and forward-looking decision that reflects our commitment to meeting the educational and workforce needs of Louisiana,” said Tony Clayton, chairman of the Southern University Board of Supervisors. “Establishing a law school in Shreveport strengthens our mission to provide access and opportunity, while positioning the Southern University System to have an even greater impact across the state.”

The proposed law school would build upon the legacy and excellence of the Southern University Law Center, further extending its reach to serve students and communities in North Louisiana and parts of Texas and Arkansas.

Alvin Washington, chancellor of Southern University Law Center, emphasized the significance of the expansion.

“This initiative represents an important opportunity to extend the Law Center’s mission and impact,” Washington said. “We are committed to producing practice-ready graduates and increasing access to legal education for students who aspire to serve their communities. Expanding into Shreveport allows us to do just that.”

The Board’s decision was met with strong support from regional leaders and Southern University Law Center alumni. Among those expressing support were Appellate Judge Shonda Stone, Louisiana State Senator Sam Jenkins, and Attorney Carl Franklin, all of whom underscored the importance of increasing access to legal education and strengthening the legal workforce in North Louisiana.

The resolution authorizes system leadership to move forward with the next phases of planning, which will include accreditation considerations, program development, and continued engagement with community and state stakeholders.

Additional details regarding timelines and implementation will be shared as the planning process advances.

item.title: Southern University advances plans to expand on-campus student housing
item.description:
The Southern University Board of Supervisors has taken a step toward expanding student housing at Southern University and A&M College, bringing the institution closer to addressing the growing demand for on-campus living.  The project encompasses two new residential buildings, which would add approximately 850 beds to the housing inventory.  One building would be dedicated to first- and second-year students, and the other would be more apartment-like residences marketed to upper-class and graduate students. 

During its meeting today, the Board approved a resolution granting preliminary approval for student housing financing involving Southern University and A&M College, the Southern University System Foundation, and the Louisiana Public Facilities Authority.   

As part of the presentation, the Board reviewed a market analysis and a residential student housing design-build report, both of which underscored the increasing need for additional housing capacity on the Baton Rouge campus. 

“This is an important step forward for Southern University and A&M College,” said Chancellor John Pierre. “The demand for student housing on our campus continues to grow, and expanding our residential capacity is critical to enhancing the student experience, supporting enrollment growth, and ensuring that our students have access to safe, modern living environments.” 

The proposed project reflects Southern University’s ongoing commitment to improving campus infrastructure and creating spaces that support student success both inside and outside the classroom. 

The approval of the resolution allows the University and its partners to proceed with the next phases, which include presentations to the state bond commission and the Louisiana Board of Regents.

item.title: Southern University mourns the passing of legendary former coach and alumnus Gerald Kimble
item.description:
Photo: Shreveport Bossier Journal


Southern University and A&M College mourns the passing of former head football coach and alumnus Gerald Kimble, who died Tuesday, March 31 at the age of 84.

Kimble leaves behind a legacy as both a student-athlete and coach whose impact extended across generations of Southern University students, student-athletes, and alumni.

“Coach Kimble was a true Jaguar — on the field, on the sidelines, and in the community,” said John K. Pierre, chancellor of Southern University and A&M College. “His legacy is one of excellence, resilience and service. He inspired generations to believe in themselves and to strive for greatness.”

Kimble first etched his name into Southern University history as the quarterback of the 1960 Jaguars, leading the team to a national Black college championship. In addition to his success on the football field, he was also a member of the 1960 Southwestern Athletic Conference (SWAC) championship baseball team — demonstrating his versatility as a student-athlete.

Following a distinguished playing career, Kimble returned to Southern as a coach, where he served as head football coach from 1989 to 1992.

Prior to coaching at Southern, Kimble made an indelible mark on high school football in Louisiana. Most notably, he transformed the Green Oaks High School football program in Shreveport, leading the team to its first winning season, district championship, and playoff appearance in 1979. His career also included a state championship run at Southern University Laboratory School in Baton Rouge in 1996, further cementing his legacy in coaching.

Kimble also remained connected to Southern through his contributions as a football commentator with the Southern University Radio Network, continuing to share his knowledge and passion for the game with Jaguar fans.

Southern University extends its deepest condolences to the Kimble family, former players, colleagues, and all who were impacted by his life and legacy. His contributions to Southern University and the broader community will not be forgotten.

item.title: LPB & Southern University Present The Inquisitor on March 17

The Inquisitor highlights the legacy of Congresswoman Barbara Jordan, shining a light on how her public influence shaped U.S. politics. From Nixon’s impeachment to civil rights battles, her voice demanded accountability, even as she privately faced struggles few ever knew about. While Jordan’s political legacy is the center of The Inquisitor, the film also looks at her personal life, exploring Jordan's intersectional identity navigating a landscape of politics and discrimination.

After the film, panelists Angela A. Allen-Bell, B. K. Agnihotri Endowed Professor at the Southern University Law Center, and Dr. Revathi Hines, Alphonse Jackson Professor of Political Science at Southern University, will offer insights in an interactive discussion to honor Jordan’s brilliance and her contributions to American democracy, while also exploring her story’s relevance to the present. Clinic leadership expressed gratitude to the Fifth Circuit, Judge Stewart, and his staff for their hospitality and for creating a meaningful experiential learning opportunity. item.title: Southern University among first HBCUs to join national Esports initiative

The initiative establishes the first dedicated, long-term competitive gaming home for HBCUs nationwide, expanding access, visibility and pathways for collegiate esports participation.

This one-of-a-kind partnership combines Urban One's cultural authority and its 80 million monthly unique reach, with PlayVS's extensive collegiate competition infrastructure, creating both visibility and access to scale. The launch of the community comes amid rapidly growing interest in collegiate esports and underscores the importance of equitable access and representation for HBCU students within the industry.

“As pioneers in the collegiate space, Southern University EDGE athletics is excited to join forces with PlayVS and Urban One,” said Christopher Turner, esports program director at Southern University. “This partnership bridges the gap between competitive gaming and the vibrant culture of HBCUs, meeting our students exactly where they are with a dedicated stage to showcase their skills and leadership.”

The National HBCU Esports Community will also leverage Urban One’s media platforms to amplify HBCU stories, esports culture and student leadership. Through this collaboration, Southern University student-gamers will have access to expanded competition opportunities, potential scholarship support and pathways into careers in technology and media.

Developed within the PlayVS College League, the three-year partnership will provide structured competition, national exposure and support for HBCU students — regardless of where a school’s esports program currently stands. Registration for the community opens in fall 2026, with the inaugural season of competition set to launch in spring 2027.

item.title: Southern University, SULC to host 'Exonerated Exhibit' during Women’s History Month
item.description:
Southern University and A&M College, in collaboration with the Louis A. Berry Institute for Civil Rights, Human Rights and Social Justice at the Southern University Law Center, will present the “Exonerated Exhibit,” featuring artwork by Becky Gottsegen, from March 3–25 at the Leon R. Tarver II Cultural and Heritage Center. Tonight will feature the "Wrongful Convictions Panel" at 5 p.m., led by law professor Angela A. Allen-Bell.
 
Held in observance of Women’s History Month, the exhibit recognizes both Gottsegen and Allen-Bell for their contributions to advancing dialogue on justice, equity and human rights through art, scholarship and advocacy.
 
Allen-Bell is known for her work addressing wrongful convictions and systemic inequities within the criminal legal system. Her research and advocacy have influenced legal scholarship, policy discussions and the lives of individuals affected by miscarriages of justice.
 
Gottsegen’s exhibit presents sculpted busts and visual narratives honoring individuals who were wrongfully convicted and later exonerated after serving a combined 726 years in prison. The installation is designed to encourage reflection and public conversation about accountability, reform and the human impact of wrongful incarceration.

item.title: Southern University Law Center Welcomes the Next Generation of Legal Leaders During the Fall 2025 Commencement Ceremony
item.description:
On Saturday, January 24, Southern University Law Center (SULC) proudly celebrated its Fall 2025 Commencement Ceremony, honoring graduates who were awarded the Juris Doctor degree during a momentous ceremony held at the Smith Brown Memorial Union. Surrounded by family, friends, faculty, and distinguished guests, the Class of 2025 marked the culmination of years of dedication, sacrifice, and perseverance.

Chancellor Alvin Washington opened the ceremony with a warm welcome, congratulating the graduates and acknowledging the support systems that helped guide them to this milestone. He commended the class for its resilience and encouraged graduates to carry forward SULC’s legacy of excellence, service, and leadership.

The keynote address was delivered by Timothy Hardy, a distinguished member of the Law Center’s Class of 1981. Hardy, who was named SULC Distinguished Alumnus in 2009 and inducted into the SULC Hall of Fame in 2012, shared reflections from his accomplished career in law and public service. In 2020, Hardy was appointed by Governor John Bel Edwards to the Governor’s Climate Initiatives Task Force, where he served as co-chair of the Manufacturing and Industry Committee and as a member of the Legal Advisory Group.

Hardy began his address by asking graduates to recognize and thank their families and friends whose encouragement and sacrifices made their success possible. “You will remember this for the rest of your life,” Hardy told the class. “You have the power to shape and change the world.”

Throughout his remarks, Hardy emphasized perseverance, purpose, and service, encouraging graduates to view challenges as opportunities for growth. He urged them to prepare diligently, embrace change, and rise after setbacks. “Embrace change because you will experience it and will benefit from it,” Hardy said. “Please remember to have empathy for your clients. You must protect their interests with zeal.”

Hardy concluded with a powerful message on leadership and character, reminding graduates that true leadership extends beyond titles. “True leadership is humble. True leadership is based on skills and character, not titles and perks,” he said. “Remain humble, resilient, passionate, empathic, and you can conquer the world.”

The ceremony concluded with closing remarks celebrating the achievements of the graduating class and officially welcoming them into the SULC alumni network as they embark on the next chapter of their legal careers.

item.title: President Shields: With Respect and Gratitude
item.description:
Dear Southern University System Community,

As you are aware, effective December 31, 2025, I will be leaving my role as president of the Southern University System.

Our students are and have always been my highest priority. They have been the focus of my time here, and they remain at the core of my personal and professional commitment.

Leadership Focus
For more than four decades in higher education, and throughout my tenure here, I have been presented with a profound opportunity to live out my “why”— the students. My highest calling is to support student success. I brought my experience and unique frame of reference to bear through three overarching pillars:

  • Improving student outcomes and enhancing student experience
  • Diversifying streams of revenue
  • Stewards of place

Accomplishments and Impact
I remain proud of what we have accomplished together over the past three and a half years. Through collaboration, strategic focus, and the tireless dedication of our faculty, staff, alumni, and partners, the Southern University System has made meaningful strides. Among our shared accomplishments:

Strengthened Enrollment and Student Success:
We reversed downward enrollment trends and established consistent year-over-year increases across our campuses. We focused intentionally on retention and progression, creating a more stable academic trajectory for students.

Comprehensive Strategic Planning:
We developed and launched Systemwide strategic priorities that came to life through collaborations with faculty, staff, alumni, and external partners.

Enhanced Physical and Academic Infrastructure:
We secured state and federal support for critical capital improvements across all campuses and elevated academic programs to better align with workforce needs.

Financial Stewardship:
We improved the System’s financial stability, expanded fundraising capacity, and strengthened relationships with donors and industry partners — setting the foundation for long-term growth.

Launch of an Unprecedented Capital Campaign:
During my tenure, we initiated the most ambitious capital campaign in the history of the Southern University System — an effort designed to secure transformative investments in academic excellence, student support, research, and campus infrastructure. With the support of alumni, corporate partners, and philanthropic friends, we have already raised significant early commitments, placing the campaign well on its way toward its bold goal of $880 million.

This momentum positions the System for long-term competitiveness and expanded opportunities for generations of students.

Expanding Research and Agricultural Innovation:
Southern University and A&M College successfully maintained the highly coveted R2 research designation, with reaffirmation in 2025 — underscoring the institution’s growing research capacity and its commitment to advancing innovation and scholarship. Additionally, we broadened the reach and impact of the Southern University Agricultural Research and Extension Center, reinforcing its role as a leader in community engagement, food security, and agricultural innovation.

Unified System Collaboration:
We worked to enhance coordination among the Baton Rouge, New Orleans and Shreveport campuses, Law Center, and SU Ag Center, reinforcing our identity as a comprehensive, interconnected family of institutions.

These achievements were not mine alone; they were the result of collective determination and shared purpose. However, there is still much to be done.

Confidence in the Future
I have sincere gratitude for the privilege of serving this great institution. My deepest thanks go to each of you — students, faculty, staff, alumni, and community partners — for your commitment to the mission of Southern University.

Together, we have moved the needle in a positive direction and strengthened the foundation of this System. The Southern University System has a long, distinguished history, and its legacy is strong. I leave with full confidence in the dedicated leaders in our System office and across our campuses and in the positive momentum we have built.

To ensure a seamless transition, I am committed to assisting the System in every way possible through the remainder of the year. I will fully support my successor and work to ensure that key initiatives and projects continue moving forward. I congratulate Dr. Orlando McMeans, chancellor of the Southern University Agricultural Research and Extension Center, on his appointment as interim president and am confident that his proven leadership, institutional knowledge, and record of accomplishment will provide steady guidance during this transition.

I look toward the future of the Southern University System with great optimism and excitement. This System is poised for even greater success, and I firmly believe its best days lie ahead.

Thank you again for your partnership, your dedication, and for allowing me the great honor of serving as your president. May you and yours have a joyous holiday season.

 

With respect and gratitude,

Dennis J. Shields
President, Southern University System

item.title: Enrollment continues upward trend across Southern University System
item.description:
The Southern University System’s most recent data reported to the Louisiana Board of Regents reflects a 4 percent increase in enrollment for the fall 2025 semester. Across Southern’s four degree-granting campuses — Southern University and A&M College, Southern University at New Orleans, Southern University Law Center, and Southern University at Shreveport — there are more than 14,000 students enrolled. This figure includes a 15 percent increase in first-time freshmen. These are preliminary enrollment numbers; final verified figures will be presented after the close of the fall 2025 semester.

“The continued growth of enrollment across our campuses is proof that Southern University continues its mission of providing an accessible, relevant educational experience,” said Dennis J. Shields, president of the Southern University System.  “Students continue to choose Southern because they see a place where they can belong and where they can flourish, ultimately impacting their communities in a positive way.”

Southern’s campuses, including the Southern University Agricultural Research and Extension Center, provide several wraparound services for students to support them on their respective academic journeys. This includes physical and mental wellness clinics, tutoring, alumni engagement, career-readiness, and a variety of student life activities.

In-demand academic programs are examined and added across the System. Recently, Southern University and A&M College launched a digital media arts program, and Southern University at New Orleans reinstated its evening and weekend program. Accolades are also plentiful, including the Southern University Law Center’s recent unprecedented first-time bar passage rate of 75 percent.

Louisiana remains the top state of residence for students across the Southern University System. Following are Texas, California, Georgia, Mississippi and Illinois. The top selected majors are nursing, business, social work, criminal justice, psychology and biology.

“This increase in enrollment is not only a testament to the hard work of our dedicated faculty, staff, and alumni, but it is also a call to action to continue to expand our investment in the services and facilities that contribute to student enrollment, retention, and successful matriculation,” Shields said.

This investment is apparent across the campuses as construction and deferred maintenance projects are plentiful. In Baton Rouge, construction continues on a $68M STEM complex, public safety building, outdoor classroom and amphitheater, and global innovation and welcome center. The Shreveport campus has broken ground on a new health, physical, and recreation complex, and the New Orleans campus has broken ground on a new building for its nursing school.

item.title: Professor Pedrioli Presents Research on Free Speech and Environmental Advocacy at Global Conference in Paris
item.description:
Southern University Law Center Professor Carlo Pedrioli recently presented his research at the Academic Days on Open Government and Digital Issues Conference, hosted by the IMODEV, the DreDis of IRJS, the Master’s degree Data Law, Digital Administrations and Open Government of the University Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne in Paris, France.

Held November 4-5, 2025, the conference welcomed more than 150 participants from 34 countries, fostering global dialogue on open government, law, and digital issues.

 "At Academic Days 2025, participants took the opportunity to discuss interdisciplinary interests related to open government and digital issues with fellow scholars from around the world, says Professor Pedrioli.  "My research project critiques recent U.K. law that provides excessive punishment for civil disobedience related to important matters of public concern, including the ongoing environmental crisis."  

Professor Pedrioli’s presentation, “Critiquing the U.K.’s Public Order Act 2023,” explored recent restrictions on protest speech in the United Kingdom, especially those affecting environmental activism. His research provides a timely critique of how modern legal frameworks can challenge free expression in democratic societies.

Pedrioli’s interest in U.K. free speech developed during the four years he spent teaching Constitutional Law there. His international experience continues to shape his comparative legal scholarship and enrich his teachings to students at the Law Center.

item.title: Priority Registration: What Students Should Know
item.description: Priority registration is giving students an opportunity to secure classes before courses reach capacity, providing an advantage as they prepare for the upcoming semester. As the registration period begins, university officials are emphasizing the importance of early enrollment to help students stay on track for graduation, avoid scheduling conflicts and ensure access to required courses. University staff say understanding the registration process and meeting with the appropriate advisors early can make a significant difference in a student’s ability to build an effective schedule. Mandy W. Green, MPA, executive assistant for the College of Humanities and Interdisciplinary Studies, said priority registration gives students an advantage because “the early bird gets the worm, so the students can get to their classes ahead of time.” However, she noted that one of the most common issues students face is that “students do not know where to go and who they should see for advising.” Green said the issue could be addressed through “more communication via email notifications and more advertisement of priority registration.” Lamyia Magee, a junior civil engineering major from Hattiesburg, Mississippi, said students can make the most of priority registration by planning ahead and understanding their degree requirements. She encouraged students, especially underclassmen, to review their degree plans, communicate regularly with academic advisors and register as early as possible. According to Magee, taking those steps can help students secure required courses, stay on track for graduation and avoid delays caused by prerequisite requirements. “Get familiar with your degree plan, communicate with your advisor, and plan ahead,” Magee said. “The decisions you make during your first few semesters can really impact the rest of your college experience.” Kennedy Alexander, a sophomore nursing major from Louisiana, said preparation and organization are key to a successful priority registration experience. She encouraged students to stay in good academic standing, pay close attention to university announcements and familiarize themselves with registration requirements before their assigned registration date. Alexander also recommended identifying backup courses in case preferred classes fill quickly. According to her, staying organized, managing time effectively and being proactive can help students navigate registration more smoothly and remain on track toward graduation. “Staying organized, managing your time, and being proactive about your education can make the registration process easier and help you stay on track toward graduation,” Alexander said. With classes filling quickly each semester, students are encouraged to take advantage of priority registration to secure the courses they need. Registering early can help students avoid scheduling conflicts, stay on track for graduation and prevent delays caused by unavailable courses. Officials emphasize that planning ahead, meeting with advisors and understanding degree requirements can help students make the most of priority registration and stay on track toward graduation.

item.title: FAFSA 2026-2027 Policy Updates
item.description: Changes to the 2026-2027 Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) are raising concerns among Southern University students as new federal regulations threaten Pell Grant eligibility and could reduce financial assistance for thousands of students who depend on aid to pay for college. The changes stem from the One Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025, with several provisions taking effect during the 2026-2027 academic year. Under the new guidelines, students with a Student Aid Index (SAI) of 14,790 or higher are no longer eligible for federal Pell Grants. Students whose entire cost of attendance is covered by non-federal scholarships or grants may also lose Pell Grant eligibility. Deshaun Fontenot, a financial aid counselor at Southern University, said the changes could have significant consequences for students who depend on financial assistance to continue their education. “A lot of students are losing Pell eligibility because of that,” Fontenot said. Fontenot explained that students receiving full scholarships may be especially affected because financial aid packages must comply with federal cost of attendance restrictions. She warned that reduced aid could leave some students with outstanding balances that may prevent them from enrolling in future semesters. “If they are not following the guidelines and they fall below the guidelines, that’s going to add to balances, and then those balances may not be able to get paid for the next semester,” Fontenot said. For students who rely on scholarships to cover living expenses and educational opportunities, the financial impact could extend far beyond tuition. Anthony Newkirk, a junior electrical engineering major at Southern University, expressed concern about how reductions in financial assistance could affect students’ academic and professional development. “For some of us, our main source of income comes from our scholarships,” Newkirk said. Newkirk explained that scholarship funds often help students pay for off-campus housing, educational materials, and professional development opportunities such as conferences. He said losing additional financial support could limit opportunities for engineering students and others pursuing career-building experiences. “Without that extra bit of money helping us get along, it just puts a strain on our development,” Newkirk said. Tytianna Smith, a junior agricultural major at Southern University, said she is particularly concerned about out-of-state students who depend heavily on financial aid and do not receive an out-of-state fee waiver. “I just know they are feeling it the most because not only are they limiting the aid, but their school costs also include out-of-state fees, which can be detrimental,” Smith said. As students prepare for the upcoming academic year, many are worried about how these changes could affect their ability to remain enrolled and take advantage of opportunities that support their academic success. Students with questions about their eligibility or financial aid awards are encouraged to contact the Southern University Office of Financial Aid for clarification on how the new regulations may affect their enrollment and educational expenses.

item.title: Tesla’s New Roadster Sparks Debate Over Future of Transportation
item.description: The unveiling of Tesla’s next-generation Roadster has sparked conversations about the future of transportation, as Southern University students and faculty weigh the possibilities of flying vehicles against concerns about safety, environmental impact, and affordability. Unveiled on Oct. 15, the redesigned electric sports car features rocket-style thrusters developed in collaboration with SpaceX. Tesla claims the technology could allow the vehicle to briefly maneuver through the air, turning a long-standing science fiction concept into a topic of serious discussion. While the idea of flying cars may seem futuristic, some believe the technology required to make them a reality is already within reach. Dr. Dwayne Jerro, associate dean of student affairs at the College of Sciences, said many technological breakthroughs begin as ideas years before technology existed to support them. “The idea comes, but it takes 20 years for the technology to catch up with the idea,” Jerro said. Jerro explained that developing vehicles capable of aerial movement would require engineers to master principles such as lift, drag and thrust. However, he noted that creating technology is only part of the challenge. Making it affordable, reliable and practical for everyday consumers could prove even more difficult. Although Jerro views the Roadster as another example of technological progress, students voiced concerns about whether the automotive industry and the public are prepared for such advancements. Ne’Kirian Guidry, a junior electrical engineering major with a minor in mathematics, said her primary concern is how flying vehicles would safely operate alongside traditional traffic.”I don’t want to see a car just taking off in the middle of the sky while we’re driving on the road or in traffic,” Guidry said. Guidry also questioned the role of automation in flying vehicles, particularly how drivers would regain control if an automated flight system failed. While intrigued by the technology, she said she would be more likely to purchase the Roadster as a collector’s item than use it as everyday transportation. Trinity Banks, a junior civil engineering major with a minor in construction management, said advancements in vehicle technology were inevitable but questioned whether society is prepared for them. “It just seems too soon for it, and I don’t think we’re ready for it,” Banks said. Banks also expressed concerns about the energy required to operate and potentially mass-produce vehicles with aerial capabilities, raising questions about the environmental and economic costs of widespread adoption. As Tesla continues developing the Roadster and plans for production to begin in 2028, its futuristic features are generating both excitement and skepticism. For Southern University students and faculty, the discussion extends beyond whether cars can fly to whether the technology can become safe, affordable and practical enough for everyday use.

item.title: White House Press Secretary Fired After Five Days on Job
item.description: The White House is once again making headlines for major staff changes. On Friday, October 16, it was announced that Press Secretary Katie Zacharia would be let go after lasting only five days in the role, setting a record for one of the shortest tenures of a press secretary. The firing comes after a string of mishaps from Zacharia, who struggled to make a strong impression on her debut. During several press briefings, she was unable to keep up with reporters’ probing questions, often fumbling over her words and displaying a lack of knowledge about the current relationship between the United States and Ukraine. It was later revealed that Zacharia had never passed the bar exam despite repeatedly referring to herself as a lawyer. The controversy deepened after she claimed, “I got it from China,” raising further questions about her credentials. Because White House officials are expected to provide accurate and trustworthy information, misrepresenting legal qualifications can damage public confidence. The disclosure also highlighted concerns about the White House’s vetting process, especially considering Zacharia was personally selected by President Trump. Such an oversight can cause great mistrust within a country. This is highly evident among university students, many of whom are preparing to vote and become more engaged in the political process. Many students had much to say on the topic. Sophomore nursing major Trinity Gilder shared her concerns, saying, “This does affect my trust. If the people aren’t prepared or qualified for their job, then why should we trust them? But at the same time, it’s a little bit not surprising due to the person we have in office.” Gilder also emphasized the importance of qualifications in government positions. “I would just say, making sure that people are qualified, and they know what they are doing, because right now, there are a lot of people in office who don’t know what they’re doing and are leading us into a hole,” Gilder added. Other students also had opinions on what should be improved. First-year law student Cierra Daniels explained, “I think that there should be less partisanship. I know when people are appointed by the president for positions, they are interviewed through Congress. And with the Trump administration, there is this undying loyalty that Republicans seem to have to him. There are a lot of things that slip through the cracks, and that’s how we ended up in this situation.” Incidents like this make it clear that changes must be made in the White House. As many young voters begin to head to the polls, it is important to have an environment where they believe in those they are electing to office. Sudden staff changes involving individuals personally selected by the president can hinder voters from fully building trust in government leadership. There must be improvements, especially if those in office want to maintain the confidence of the public and remain in office.

item.title: From the gridiron to greatness: SU alum's film earns festival selection
item.description: After spending nearly two decades playing football, Glenn Brown III is pursuing a different creative path. The 2023 Southern University and A&M College graduate is now making his mark as a filmmaker, with his psychological thriller, "You Should’ve Looked Closer," selected for the 37th New Orleans Film Festival. For Brown, the transition from athletics to filmmaking is about more than changing careers. It is about challenging expectations and finding an identity beyond the sport that shaped much of his life. “I knew sports was something that I was good at. I knew it wasn’t who I was,” Brown said. Courtesy: glennabrowniii/Instagram   Brown grew up in Lutcher, LA and began playing football since he was five years old, including his time as a four-year starter at Southern as a defensive back. He said moving on from a sport that had occupied so much of his life was not easy. “It’s hard to focus on something for almost 20 years, and then just move on from it,” Brown said. “That’s hard. People don’t mention that enough.” He also recognized how expectations can shape the paths athletes believe are available to them, particularly Black athletes. “As an athlete with our skin color, they want to put you in a box, like you’re an athlete. That’s all you are and that’s all you’re going to be,” Brown said. “If you don’t make it to the NFL, you’re going to be a coach and I just wasn’t going for that.” Rather than limit himself to the future others might have expected, Brown looked to entertainers and filmmakers who had successfully moved between creative fields. He cited Ice Cube’s transition from music to filmmaking and acting, along with Will Smith’s career in television and film, as examples that inspired him. Brown also connected with the journey of filmmaker Ryan Coogler, who played football before pursuing a career in film, and actor LaKeith Stanfield, whom Brown worked alongside as a stand-in on the film "I Love Boosters." Courtesy: Glenn Brown III Finding his voice through film Brown’s interest in filmmaking began long before "You Should’ve Looked Closer." He said his father made films and music videos in New Orleans, while his grandmother regularly bought movies for the family to watch. Those early experiences helped develop his interest in storytelling. While at Southern, Brown studied mass communication with a focus in journalism. He initially wanted to pursue sports broadcasting, inspired by watching sports commentators, including Stephen A. Smith, Shannon Sharpe, Skip Bayless and Ryan Clark. Balancing academics with the demands of being a starting football player was challenging. Brown said he struggled in the classroom while focusing heavily on football and creating YouTube content. The possibility of becoming academically ineligible and losing his scholarship forced him to take his studies more seriously. He said the experience helped him develop the discipline and accountability he now relies on as a filmmaker. “I had to step into that role and learn how to direct myself, and hold myself accountable,” Brown said. Although he enjoys writing and acting more than directing, Brown took on multiple responsibilities to complete his first film. He wrote, directed, produced and acted in his film “You Should’ve Looked Closer.” Brown established his production company, Elephant Hill Media, in 2024 while studying acting at Catapult Studios in Atlanta. He said creating his own projects also gave him a way to keep working during periods when acting opportunities were limited. “I want to own something,” Brown said. “It’s just good to have ownership and, you know, build from the ground up.” A film about mental health and perception “You Should’ve Looked Closer” is an experimental psychological thriller centered on a young man named King. The film explores mortality, memory and perception through a nontraditional editing style that invites audiences to interpret what they see. Brown said he wanted to address suicide without depicting the act itself. Courtesy: Glenn Brown III/Elephant Hill Media The idea became meaningful to Brown when he wrote the film in the summer of 2025. He said several people in his hometown had taken their lives, including people connected to St. James High School, where he attended. Brown said he has long been drawn to stories that challenge audiences and spark conversations about uncomfortable subjects. With his first film, he wanted to explore the experiences of people coping with the loss of a loved one who struggled with their mental health. He also hopes the film encourages viewers who may be struggling to recognize that people around them care about them. Brown said he wants audiences to develop their own interpretations of the experimental film, while also considering the lives and relationships affected by suicide. Looking ahead When Brown submitted “You Should’ve Looked Closer” to film festivals, he did not expect it to be selected. He recalled receiving the notification while sitting in a barbershop and smiling as he processed the news. “I had no expectations at all,” he said. The selection gave Brown an opportunity to introduce his work to a wider audience as he continues developing his craft. He is now writing a feature-length supernatural horror film set in New Orleans. Brown hopes to secure at least $50,000 in funding to make the project and pay the people involved, with an emphasis on working with Louisiana talent. He also wants to tell stories that reflect the state beyond familiar stereotypes, exploring both its positive and difficult realities through a Black Southern Gothic perspective. “There just aren’t enough films about Louisiana,” Brown said. “I want to make a movie and make a film about Louisiana, the good parts and the bad parts, and have really uncomfortable conversations.” For Southern students pursuing interests outside their original career plans, Brown encourages them to take lessons from their education and apply them to whatever path they choose. “It’s always something you could take away from anything that you decide to study,” he said. “You Should’ve Looked Closer” is scheduled to screen Oct. 23 at 8 p.m. and Oct. 26 at 3 p.m. at the Contemporary Arts Center in New Orleans as part of the 37th New Orleans Film Festival. Tickets are available for purchase by clicking here.

item.title: Southern University professor selected for 2026 Alex Trebek Legacy Fellowship
item.description: Darrell Roberson, co-director and chair of the digital media arts program and Title III activity director at Southern University and A&M College, has been selected for the 2026 Alex Trebek Legacy Fellowship. The fellowship, awarded by the Television Academy Foundation in Hollywood, California, supports educators from community colleges and minority-serving institutions in attending the foundation’s annual Media Educators Conference.  The three-day conference will take place Oct. 21-23 at the Television Academy’s North Hollywood campus, connecting college educators with television industry professionals through seminars on the art, science and business of television. “I’m honored to be one of 18 faculty members from universities around the country selected as a 2026 Alex Trebek Legacy Fellow and to represent Southern University,” Roberson said. “I look forward to bringing back ideas and connections that can help us build our program, prepare our students, and benefit the university.” Roberson and fellow co-director Harry Anderson Sr. lead Southern’s digital media arts program. The program is designed to equip students with both creative and technical skills, and combines hands-on production experience with a strong foundation in theory, humanities, and digital technologies. Roberson teaches video editing and sports production and helps develop the studios where students gain hands-on experience in digital media. This year, Roberson helped organize Southern’s inaugural Digital Media Arts Conference and second annual Digital Media Arts Symposium, bringing students together with working media professionals. Established in 2021 by the Harry & Judy Friedman Family Foundation, the Alex Trebek Legacy Fellowships honor the late Alex Trebek, longtime host of the television game show Jeopardy! The program provides financial support to educators seeking to enhance their teaching and strengthen connections between academic programs and the television industry.

item.title: Former Southern University professor tied to Nobel Prize-winning discovery
item.description: Southern University and A&M College professor emeritus Ali R. Fazely, Ph.D. has contributed to research connected to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the groundbreaking scientific project at the center of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. Fazely collaborated with Francis Halzen, Ph.D., a University of Wisconsin–Madison physicist who received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin. The American Institute of Physics announced the recognition Oct. 6. Located at the South Pole, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory uses more than 5,000 optical sensors embedded in approximately one cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice to detect faint flashes of light produced when neutrinos interact with matter. These nearly massless particles can travel vast distances through the universe, carrying information about some of its most energetic events. The discovery of high-energy neutrinos from astrophysical sources gave scientists a new way to study distant cosmic events beyond traditional observations using light. Fazely has led Southern’s IceCube-related research activities since 1997, working with graduate students, post-doctoral researchers and scientific collaborators. His team’s work has focused on detector simulations, rare particle decays, supernova neutrinos and high-energy neutrino interaction cross sections. Fazely said Southern’s participation in the international collaboration highlights the role historically Black colleges and universities can play in advancing scientific research. “Southern University's participation demonstrates that HBCUs can be active contributors to these efforts, not simply observers of discoveries made elsewhere,” said Fazely. Southern’s research has helped support the scientific work behind the observatory through computer simulations that model how neutrinos interact with matter, how charged particles travel through ice and how light reaches the detector’s optical sensors. These models help researchers interpret the signals IceCube records, reconstruct neutrino energies and directions, and assess potential improvements to the detector. The university’s research group has developed simulations for the existing IceCube detector, the IceCube Upgrade and the proposed IceCube-Gen2 observatory. Recent efforts have focused on supernova-neutrino simulations and future detector configurations that could help scientists identify astrophysical signals and investigate physical processes that have not yet been observed. Fazely’s research also includes studies of rare particle decays and high-energy neutrino interactions. A study exploring the possibility of observing the rare decay of an eta particle into a neutrino-antineutrino pair was published in Physical Review D in 2010. In 2019, the team published research in Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics introducing a Prime-Index parametrization of neutrino-nucleon and proton-proton cross sections. The research program has also created opportunities for Southern students to participate in advanced scientific investigations. Fazely said two students, Cheng Guo and Aaron Richard, completed Master of Science degrees through IceCube-related research, while graduate student Justin Mitchell is currently involved in the program. Through their involvement, students gain experience in particle physics, astrophysics, computer programming, statistical analysis and large-scale scientific simulations. They also become familiar with the research methods and scientific standards used in major international collaborations, preparing them for doctoral studies, research careers, national laboratories and technology-related professions. For Fazely, the program’s impact extends beyond scientific findings to the development of future researchers. “I am particularly proud that our program has combined scientific research with the education and mentoring of young scientists," he said. "In my view, that is one of Southern University's most important contributions to the future of physics.”
